newsitem.title: CYPRUS: North Cyprus to reform economy under Turkey deal.
newsitem.headline: North Cyprus to reform economy under Turkey deal.

text.p: Northern Cyprus, boosted by a $250 million credit deal with its sponsor Turkey, is preparing to make sweeping structural changes to improve its battered economy and survive in international isolation for many years to come.

"With a protocol we signed with Turkey on January 3 the cash problems regarding public finance are to some extent diminished," said Serdar Denktash, deputy prime minister of the Turkish Cypriot government that is recognised only by Turkey.
"The cash is not directly for paying debt, it is to develop the economy," Denktash, son of Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash, told Reuters.
"Legislative changes, privatisation, are all part of a big plan we are discussing... If we do it right, I expect improvement in 1997 public funding," he said.

The economic picture in north Cyprus is not rosy. The budget deficit jumped from 811,928 million lira ($7.2 million) in 1994 to 4,388,003 million lira ($39 million) in 1995, according to latest figures. And the enclave is weighed down by high annual inflation -- 87.5 percent last year, from 72.2 percent in 1996.

Per capita gross national product fell to $3,093 in 1994 from $3,447 in 1990. In comparison, the Greek Cypriot economy is flourishing, with earnings per capita of over $12,000 and single-digit inflation.

Denktash said the details of the Turkish-sponsored plan should be drawn up this month. He said the lumbering bureaucracy must be slimmed, an effective incentive system introduced to boost production, and the outdated pension system reformed.

"It has been a vicious circle. The economy must grow so the state sector becomes a relatively small portion of this. For this you need investment, you need resources, and in this tiny country there are no resources for investment," said Salih Cosar, the breakway state's finance minister. "So we need this help from Turkey."
North Cyprus has been split from the Greek Cypriot south since 1974 when Turkey invaded in response to a coup in Nicosia engineered by the military junta then ruling Greece.
The economy of the Turkish north, recognised as a republic only by Ankara, has struggled to stand up under embargo.

In recent years it has taken further blows from the 1991 Gulf War, the collapse in the same year of Polly Peck International, a fruits-to-electronics conglomerate owned by Turkish Cypriot tycoon Asil Nadir, and an effective ban by the European Union on trade with the Turkish Cypriots in 1994.

The EU ban killed a flourishing trade in citrus fruit and hurt clothing output. International isolation means no direct flights or marine routes except from Turkey, hampering trade and tourism. Recent droughts have also harmed the ailing agricultural sector.

Frequent standoffs with Greek Cypriots have also hit tourism. After a violent biker protest in Nicosia last year, many tourists cancelled their visits, economic officials say. Tourism income, $219 million in 1995, was $180 million in 1996.

To add to its woes, the economy was hit badly by a Turkish financial crisis in 1994 that sent inflation and interest rates spiralling -- the two economies are closely linked and northern Cyprus uses the beleaguered Turkish lira as its currency.
"We suffer from Turkey's economic problems," said Ahmet Zeki Buluc, head of the State Planning Organisation.

"We can never expect to cut inflation to half of Turkey's. But we can't call this a burden when all we have to rely on is Turkey. But if we do nothing to combat structural problems, we will suffer even when Turkey's economy improves."

Economic officials say in the 1970s, north Cyprus emulated Turkey's early republican years and set up large state firms. In its isolation, the private sector was unable to grow. And following the collapse of Polly Peck International, a successful private enterprise, the state sector became seen as the only safe place to work.
Cosar said payments to the veterans of fighting against Greek Cypriots in the early 1960s and in 1974 and the families of those who died in the clashes added to the state's burden.
"In all, the treasury is only left with 38 lira in every 100 it collects -- to work an economy on this is impossible."
In 1991, the country's economy shrank by 5.3 percent. It managed to grow in 1992 and 1993, but it shrank again in 1994, by 3.7 percent, and it has grown negligibly since then.
After the credit deal, Cosar said Turkey and northern Cyprus should sign a free trade deal like the European Union.
Denktash said it was time to dismiss excuses and learn to live with the political situation as it is.

"Until now we have looked only at disadvantages -- not being recognised, embargoes, the political problems. It is time to try and turn this into an advantage," he said. "Taiwan, after all, is not recognised, but it is developing." ($=112,200 Turkish lira)
